learn.why: Tap a word, get a bottom sheet with one line and a shield icon, close it, keep playing. It stays in the thing I am already doing. B is a big list of 7 names before I have even chosen, that is homework. C's full page is a wall of text with a map and 4 bios, I would swipe it away. A's 'In your game' line (front line 52 of 100) is the only bit that felt like a game.
would_turn_off: brief me on each new crisis
the italic serif crisis paragraph itself (too much text)
unknown_terms_i_saw: Moscow calls it a basis (Moscow = Russia?)
kill_criteria_hit: Q3 for B: I could not tell what the list did for the choice, scores 2 for me
C's deep briefing is a wall of text: deal breaker

answers.Q1: Do not know or could not explain: Donetsk oblast (later, maybe never), fortress belt (now, it sounds cool), Kramatorsk and Sloviansk (never), demilitarising (never, I guess no army), internationally run economic zone (later), 'a basis' (never), midterms (now, a little, I heard it on TikTok but not what it does here), accepting in principle (never), referendum (later, I think it is a vote), the Rada (never). I know Ukraine, Russia, Putin, Trump, Zelensky, US.
answers.Q2: A: yes. The dotted underlines are small, and the tap sheet is quick, like a tooltip in Clash Royale. B: no. A button with '7 names' is a chore, and the panel covers half the screen. C: maybe. The 'i' idea is fine but the 'What is going on here' page looks like a school worksheet, though the map is cool.
answers.Q3: Fortress belt, variant A, 4/5. I tapped the underlined phrase and got 'Four fortified cities... Ukraine's strongest line in the east' plus 'Front line 52 of 100'. The one read worked. 'More' and 'Codex' buttons I would ignore.
answers.Q4: A 4, B 2, C 4 (the 'i' is quiet, but I wonder if I would even see it).
answers.Q5: Some help. Guide me sounds like for kids, I know this is a lie. Turn off first: the 'brief me on each new crisis' and the codex toast. Underlines I would keep.
answers.Q6: No, I would not open it before choosing, I want to pick and see what happens. If I did, the one-line summary first, then the map. Who is who has Trump and Putin, which I know, so I would skip it. Missing: what happens if I say yes or no, in 5 words.
answers.Q7: '18 of 31 met' is a bit like collecting cards, so I might open a few NEW entries, but only if it pings. After the game I would look at it for a screenshot, probably not read. Medium care.
answers.Q9: A. Make the sheet only ever one line and one 'In your game' fact, with no More button unless I ask.
answers.Q10: 'As of Nov 2026' I would not notice. One wrong fact I would not catch, but if my teacher caught it I would stop quoting it. Facts flagged: none, I would not know.

worldmap.why: Numbered fires 1 to 5 tell me where to tap first and the stability colors (orange-red shaky) look like danger on a map. A on 2026 has lots of red war icons and a card but it felt noisy. B also has a bigger list of the situations as chips with numbers below the globe.
kill_criteria_hit: Q3 phone: A 2026 shows the Ukraine label sitting under a pin and Kazakhstan label near pins, a bit crowded
A 2026 bottom sheet covers the list and the era buttons, text behind it is a mess

answers.Q1: S1/S3 A 1960: January 1960 is in the header. I see Soviet Union in red, a blue West, France with an icon, Berlin pin. A war icon near France/Algeria. B 1960 told me faster, because the pins have numbers and the list says 'Divided Berlin, Algerian' right under. B was faster.
answers.Q2: Yes, different. 1960 has a sepia/orange feel and names like Soviet Union and 'Nigeria (British)' which is a cool detail. 2026 has Russia and Ukraine. Between eras the year text and country names changed. I would not notice an anachronism, I do not know the old borders.
answers.Q3: Mostly readable on the phone. In A 2026 the Ukraine label is jammed against a pin, and Russia/Kazakhstan are big but fine. Yemen sits right on a pin in A. B 2026 is cleaner. Missing: I looked for Taiwan and China and did not see them on the phone globe.
answers.Q4: The yellow one with the radiation-like icon near India, I think it is a nuclear thing. The anchor pins I guess are ships or the sea. Dashed vs solid I would not notice at this size. Red war icon yes, that I get. The dotted lines I did not notice.
answers.Q5: I saw a small purple arrow on the left edge, in both. I would expect it to spin the globe to that spot. Taiwan, Cuba, Korea I did not look for.
answers.Q6: A card next to the pin on a phone is the bottom sheet: it shows 3 countries with a number each (Holding 57) and two buttons 'Lead Russia', 'Lead Ukraine' and the big orange Play. That is clear and fun, I like picking a side. But it covers the buttons below. I do not know what 'Holding 57' means.
answers.Q7: Five numbered fires by default. It is already a lot on a phone. I would not flip the switch, maybe once if I was bored.
answers.Q8: Stability coloring: I could see shaky orange-red vs slate, it looks like a heat map, which I get right away. Blocs colouring I did not know the colors mean. I could tell most colors apart, the orange vs red a little less.
answers.Q9: Cool moment, 1 second is fine and the year rolling is satisfying. I would switch eras more because of it, at least to show a friend. If it was longer than 1.5 s it would be a delay.
answers.Q10: Yes bigger than a normal menu, but on the phone the globe is half the screen and the pins are tappable, about thumb size, fine. The 2026 pins are a bit small and close near Yemen and Iran.
answers.Q11: B. Numbered fires are a to-do list for my thumb. One change: make the number pins bigger and tap-to-go on the rim marker, and say in 3 words what the colors mean.

verbatim: Just let me tap the thing and blow stuff up, give me one line if I get stuck and put the big orange button right there.
